articles.title: Man guilty of rape in Somerset after woman's secret recording
articles.summary: Police said the recording, in which she is heard saying "no", provided key evidence.
articles.body:
A man has been found guilty of raping a woman whose mobile phone recording provided key evidence for police.

Ayman Al-Shammari, 28, was found guilty by a jury at Bristol Crown Court on Friday after a trial.

The court heard Al-Shammari and the woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, started to have consensual sex on 14 November 2025 but he did not stop after she asked.

She was able to unlock her phone and record what was happening, the court heard, and that she was described as sounding in pain, upset and crying.

Fireworks 'exciting but scary' for autistic people

Ex-football chief admits offences linked to woman's drugging and rape by husband

What you need to know about upcoming M5 closures

Al-Shammari, a Kuwaiti national living in Taunton, was remanded in custody to be sentenced on 27 November.

Al-Shammari denied rape but was found guilty by a majority verdict.

The jury heard Al-Shammari had known the woman for a few weeks, having met her on a night out, and they had slept together once.

On the night of the incident, he tried to persuade her to come out for the evening and when she said no, he convinced her to let him come to her home.

After a few drinks he asked to stay the night and she agreed to let him sleep on the sofa, telling him they were just friends.

The court was told Al-Shammari went to the woman's room and they did start to have consensual sex, but the woman later told police she was feeling "more and more uncomfortable". She said she asked him to stop but he did not.

The jury heard the recording in which the woman said "no" and "I don't like it".

In his police interview, Al-Shammari denied rape and told officers the woman had wanted sex but the positions they tried hurt her so he stopped.

A spokesperson for Avon and Somerset Police said: "Rape is a crime which often happens behind closed doors, leaving a jury to decide which of the two people is telling the truth.

"This is an unusual case as the survivor provided key evidence by recording the attack.

"Avon and Somerset Police remain committed to thoroughly investigating reports of sexual offences, supporting victims and pursuing offenders through the criminal justice system.

"The circumstances of this case highlight the importance of consent in sexual relationships.

"No means no, whether you've had consensual sex before or not. If you have any doubt about their consent, stop."

articles.title: Connecticut volunteers are attaching eelgrass seeds to living clams to restore meadows that have shrunk by 90%; after an early 178% rise in coverage, the team is testing rice-paper planting with 300,000 seeds
articles.summary: In the shallow waters of Long Island Sound, Connecticut volunteers are using an unlikely pair of helpers to bring back an underwater forest: live clams
articles.body: In the shallow waters of Long Island Sound, Connecticut volunteers are using an unlikely pair of helpers to bring back an underwater forest: live clams and eelgrass seeds. Researchers and community members are gluing seeds to clam shells, then releasing the clams at carefully chosen sites where they burrow into the seabed and effectively plant the seeds. The approach, known as Seeds of Eelgrass Attached to Shellfish (SEAS), has already produced encouraging early results, with drone imagery showing a 178 percent increase in eelgrass meadow coverage after the 2025 planting. The work matters because eelgrass meadows in and around Long Island Sound have declined by more than 90 percent since the 1980s, according to Save the Sound. These underwater grasslands shelter young fish and invertebrates, filter water, absorb excess nutrients, stabilise shorelines, and release oxygen. Restoring them is difficult, but the clam planting method may offer a practical, nature-based way to rebuild habitat that has all but disappeared. Read more about it here:Why eelgrass is worth savingEelgrass, or Zostera marina, is a flowering plant that grows entirely underwater in shallow coastal areas. Its long green leaves form dense meadows that provide food and shelter for many marine species, including young fish and invertebrates. The plants also help reduce coastal erosion by stabilising sediment and absorbing wave energy.Besides habitat, eelgrass is important for water quality. It brings in more nutrients, filters particles out of the water and adds oxygen to the environment around it. Save the Sound describes the meadows as interconnected with healthy fish populations, clean water, and resilient shorelines, making their loss a concern for the entire Long Island Sound ecosystem.The decline has been driven by decades of pressure from reduced water quality, warming waters, and coastal development. As the meadows disappeared, the benefits they provided weakened as well. Restoring them is not simply about planting a pretty underwater plant. It is about rebuilding a living system that supports marine life and protects vulnerable coastlines.Clams become underwater gardenersTraditional eelgrass restoration can be challenging because seeds and young plants often fail to establish themselves in the right place. A different approach is the SEAS method, which uses clams as natural planting tools. Volunteers glue eelgrass seeds to the shells of live clams, which are then released into the Sound at designated restoration sites. The clams, once submerged, carry the seeds down into the sediment as they burrow. As they dig, they place the seeds close to the seabed, where they have a better chance of germinating and growing into eelgrass. The process also recreates a natural relationship between the two species: clams help oxygenate the sediment, while eelgrass catches bits of food that can benefit the clams.The idea was conceived by Robert Vasiluth, founder of SAVE Environmental, and is now being tested by a consortium stewarded through the Connecticut National Estuarine Research Reserve. The on-the-water team includes Save the Sound, Connecticut College, Remote Ecologist, the University of Connecticut, Cornell Cooperative Extension, and Stony Brook University.An early sign of successIn fall 2025, the team planted 30,000 seed-carrying clams in four experimental plots off Duck Island near Westbrook, Connecticut. The site was large enough for researchers to monitor progress from the air using drone imagery. When they checked the results in 2026, they found that eelgrass meadow coverage had increased by 178 percent. Bill Lucey, Save the Sound’s Long Island Soundkeeper, said, as per Popular Science, that the method appears to have worked, but he cautioned that the team needs the plants to survive for three years before declaring full success. Even so, he described the generation of plants as incredible and said the clam planting approach showed real promise after many earlier failed attempts at restoration.The early results are important because eelgrass restoration has often struggled to produce lasting meadows. By letting clams do the planting, the team is working with natural behavior rather than trying to force seeds into place. The method also allows volunteers to participate directly in restoration, turning a technical conservation project into a community effort.Rice paper, coral glue, and 300,000 seedsThis season, the team is refining how the seeds are attached. In 2025, volunteers used a glue commonly applied in coral reef restoration to fix seeds to clam shells. But Connecticut College biologist Maria Rosa found that wet pieces of rice paper, the kind used for spring rolls, produced better germination rates when used to seal seeds against the shell.The updated method places 10 to 20 eelgrass seeds on the top of each clam, adds a small circle of coral glue, and covers the seeds with a wet rice-paper stamp. The glue holds the paper in place until it dissolves underwater, releasing the seeds beside the clam. The rice paper also keeps the seeds moist during preparation and deployment.The team is aiming to release 10,000 clams carrying 300,000 seeds this season. Volunteers helped prepare the seed-carrying clams earlier this week, demonstrating how local residents can play a direct role in restoring the Sound. Save the Sound says the project has been able to expand thanks to support from 11th Hour Racing’s grant program, which has allowed more dives to collect reproductive eelgrass shoots filled with seeds.A test for the future of the soundThe next few years will determine whether the early gains become a lasting recovery. Researchers will need to confirm that the young eelgrass survives, spreads, and forms stable meadows rather than disappearing after a single season. Still, the 178 percent increase in coverage gives the team a reason to believe the clam-assisted method could become a valuable restoration tool.If successful, the approach could help restore habitat throughout Long Island Sound, improving conditions for fish, shellfish and other marine life while bolstering shorelines against erosion. It also shows how science, community volunteering and creative problem solving can come together in restoration. In Connecticut, the future of eelgrass may depend on a simple but clever idea: letting clams do the planting.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Avengers Assemble! US rolls out Stinger missiles to shield Trump's Florida estate from drone threats
articles.summary: The United States has deployed Avenger short-range air defence systems armed with Stinger missiles around President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in
articles.body: The United States has deployed Avenger short-range air defence systems armed with Stinger missiles around President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, adding another layer of protection against potential aerial threats, including drones and low-flying aircraft.According to a report by The War Zone (TWZ), the systems were deployed around two weeks before October 30, following a request from the US Secret Service. The deployment was carried out by the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) and US Northern Command (USNORTHCOM).The missile systems have been positioned at multiple locations around the estate, including a floating platform in Lake Worth Lagoon, a nearby beach and Donald J Trump International Airport, approximately three miles west of Mar-a-Lago. Photographs published by TWZ show multiple Avenger systems deployed at these locations.NORAD and USNORTHCOM have also confirmed deploying counter-unmanned aircraft system (C-UAS) capabilities as part of the security arrangement. These systems are designed to detect, identify and track drones that could pose a threat to the president or restricted airspace.The deployment comes amid heightened security concerns over potential aerial threats and follows a series of airspace violations around Palm Beach. According to TWZ, more than 160 aircraft and drones have breached restricted airspace over the area since October 2025.What is the Avenger air defence system?The AN/TWQ-1 Avenger is a mobile, short-range air defence system developed by Boeing for the US Army to protect military forces and strategic locations against low-altitude aerial threats.Mounted on an M1097-series High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle (HMMWV), commonly known as a Humvee, the system combines surface-to-air missiles, a machine gun and advanced target-detection and tracking equipment on a single mobile platform.According to the US Army's Weapon Systems Handbook 2020-2021, the Avenger is designed to engage unmanned aerial systems (UAS), cruise missiles, helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft operating at low altitudes. It can operate during both day and night, in adverse weather conditions and while the vehicle is moving.The system is operated by a two-member crew and features a rotating turret equipped with two missile launcher pods, each carrying four FIM-92 Stinger surface-to-air missiles, giving it a total capacity of eight ready-to-fire missiles.Each Stinger missile uses infrared guidance to lock onto the heat signature of an aerial target and independently guide itself after launch. This fire-and-forget capability allows the operator to engage a target without having to continuously guide the missile. The Avenger also carries an M3P .50-calibre automatic machine gun, which provides an additional weapon for engaging close-range aerial threats and ground targets. The machine gun has a basic ammunition load of 250 rounds.The US Army handbook lists the system's target-tracking range at approximately 10 km, while its Stinger missiles have an engagement range of more than 6 km. The M3P machine gun has an engagement range of more than 1 km.Drones emerge as growing threat to Trump's securityThe growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in modern warfare has emerged as an additional security concern for US President Donald Trump, prompting authorities to strengthen aerial protection around his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida.The proliferation of relatively inexpensive drones, including first-person-view (FPV) and fibre-optic-controlled systems, has made it increasingly difficult to detect and counter potential aerial threats. According to The War Zone, Iran has both used and supplied such weapons, raising concerns about the possibility of their use against high-security locations.The threat is particularly significant because Mar-a-Lago is located close to the Atlantic coastline, potentially exposing the estate to aerial threats approaching from the sea.The War Zone noted that long-range kamikaze drones, which are designed to crash into targets carrying explosive payloads, could pose a particular challenge. Unlike conventional aircraft, small drones can fly at low altitudes and may be harder to detect using traditional air surveillance systems.

articles.title: Indian national pleads guilty to $227-million medicare fraud in US over fake Covid-19 test kit claims
articles.summary: Syed Murtuza Kablazada faces justice for a massive healthcare fraud involving fraudulent COVID-19 test claims that swindled Medicare out of over $220 million.
articles.body: An Indian national has pleaded guilty in the US to two counts of health care fraud for his role in a $227 million scheme that used the personal information of hundreds of thousands of Medicare beneficiaries to submit false claims for COVID-19 test kits.Syed Murtuza Kablazada, 36, who lived in Des Plaines, Illinois, caused three Chicago-area laboratories to bill Medicare for test kits that beneficiaries had neither requested nor received, according to the US Department of Justice (DOJ).Court documents show that Kablazada and his co-conspirators acquired three laboratories, Chicago Care, V Care and Al-Ameer, over six months beginning in January 2023.They then paid approximately $11 million to a telemarketing company based in Pakistan to obtain personally identifiable information belonging to hundreds of thousands of Medicare beneficiaries. The information was used to submit fraudulent claims worth $227 million for COVID-19 test kits.Medicare paid approximately $136 million against those claims, although the kits were never requested by or shipped to the beneficiaries, the DOJ said.Investigators said Kablazada and his associates used overseas money transfers and unlicensed money transmitters to conceal their involvement and distribute the proceeds. articles.title: Education under fire: Gaza’s children face death on their way to school
articles.summary: Children have faced Israeli bombs and sniper fire since the academic year resumed in Gaza.
articles.body:
Gaza City — Mohammed Hamad, 14, was on his way home from school in Deir el-Balah on October 17 when an Israeli strike targeted the road he was travelling along.

He had finished classes at the makeshift school and was walking home through the al-Baraka neighbourhood with his 10-year-old brother, Abdullah. Mohammed was killed in the strike along with another man. Abdullah survived.

Mohammed was Riyad Hamad’s third child, an eighth-grade student among the top pupils in his class. His loss is difficult for the 44-year-old father to comprehend.

“He was not just my son, he was my friend,” Hamad told Al Jazeera from his family tent in Deir el-Balah. “He was doing so well. May God have mercy on him.”

The family has struggled to come to terms with the death of a boy whose schoolwork and achievements had been a source of pride.

“Mohammed used to ask me: ‘How am I with you?’ I swear, I never asked him for anything more,” he said.

The loss has also left a deep mark on Abdullah, who now fears losing his father, too.

“He has become very afraid of going to school. They used to go together every day and come back together. Now he cannot come to terms with having to go on his own,” Hamad said.

“We are living in fear. When I go out into the streets, I swear I am afraid. Even when I am walking or sitting in a car, my heart is filled with fear … Why should our children have to live with this constant fear and anxiety, even until the last moment?

“Enough is enough. The child is supposed to bury his father, not the father bury his child. They have turned the order of things upside down.”

The gradual return of children to school – even in makeshift classrooms and tents – had offered families in Gaza some hope of restoring a sense of normality after years of disruptions.

But Israeli air raids and sniper fire have continued, despite a ceasefire being established last October for Gaza. Since then, Israel has killed at least 1,574 Palestinians and injured 5,687 in Gaza, according to the enclave’s Ministry of Health.

The academic year resumed in Gaza on September 19, after nearly three years of disruptions caused by Israel’s war – and with it came more Israeli strikes.

Ten children aged from six to 16 and a teacher were killed between October 18 and 24. In a statement last Sunday, the Ministry of Education said that two girls were wounded during morning assembly at Muradiya School in Jabalia on October 21. Five students were also injured, some critically, in an attack on the Islamic University campus in Gaza City on Sunday.

The ministry called for urgent international action to protect students, schools and universities in Gaza.

The risks are particularly high for schools located near the so-called “Yellow Line”, a point that divided Gaza’s territory between Israeli and Palestinian control as part of the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. The line has moved westward to give Israel control of more than 65 percent of Gaza, according to the United Nations, up from the 53 percent agreed upon a year ago

At least 66 Palestinian children have been killed close to the Yellow Line, and pupils and teachers travelling near this zone remain in mortal danger from Israeli snipers and bombs.

On October 21, Suad Abd Rabbo, a fourth-grade student, went to school carrying her bag and books. Not long afterwards, her older sister rushed home shouting that Suad had been shot.

“I ran out barefoot,” Suad’s mother, Aliaa Abd Rabbo, recalled. “When I saw her, I was confused. I didn’t know what to do. She was bleeding, crying and screaming.”

The bullet struck Suad above the knee and lodged in a sensitive area close to her nerves and tendons. She was rushed to hospital, where doctors warned that trying to remove it could cause paralysis. They operated on Suad but were still unable to extract the bullet, which remains in her leg.

Abd Rabbo remembers when Suad came round from the anaesthesia after surgery and started reciting a passage she had been preparing for a school dictation exercise.

“‘O symbol of generosity and resilience … When I feel tired, I sit under an olive tree in the yard of our home, and feel rested after the exhaustion,” her mother recalled her saying.

Suad has since been discharged from hospital and has returned to her tent, where she remains unable to walk or move around. She needs surgery abroad to fully recover, but with Israel tightly controlling exit and entry from Gaza, her prospects of proper treatment are remote.

“Suad is now deeply frustrated. She cries and asks: ‘Why did this happen to me? Why was I targeted? What did I do?’” Abd Rabbo said.

Israeli tanks, military vehicles and cranes regularly open fire close to their tent in northern Gaza, particularly after sunset. Families often have to lie flat on the ground for hours to avoid the stray bullets that ricochet through the camp.

“My heart hurts when I send the girls to school. I told my husband I regret coming back from the south,” Abd Rabbo said about their return home to Jabalia after fleeing to Deir el-Balah during the war.

Another girl was also injured on the same day as Suad as students at Muradiya School were preparing for assembly at about 10:30am, Naim Aloush, the school’s principal, said.

“The girls had formed two lines … one suddenly screamed and fell to the ground … another girl standing nearby was struck by a bullet in her side,” she told Al Jazeera.

Teachers rushed to the girls and found that Suad had been shot while the second pupil, Amina Khader, a fifth-grade student, sustained a minor injury to her abdomen.

Aloush said the shooting sent fear through the school, with parents rushing to collect their children.

Pupils who had witnessed the incident were left terrified, and the school saw a marked increase in absenteeism in the days that followed.

The principal sees this incident as part of wider dangers facing the school in the al-Ghubari area, west of Jabalia al-Balad, consisting of 20 educational tents and serving about 1,000 pupils in the surrounding community, close to the Yellow Line.

Aloush said stray bullets or projectiles – from Israeli artillery, quadcopter drones and snipers – still regularly hit the school.

“Education is under fire, and our whole lives are under fire. At any moment, there can be gunfire. It is not light … it comes down like rain,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Every day, I come to school with my hand over my heart, afraid that one of my pupils or a member of the teaching staff might be hit.”

Amina, the other child injured along with Suad, has been left deeply traumatised by the incident, her father, Khaled Khader, said.

Khader said he rushed to the school after hearing that Amina had been injured and carried his daughter to a nearby clinic.

“There was terror, absolute terror. My daughter was in shock. She broke down, started screaming and collapsed,” Khader told Al Jazeera.

“Thank God she is safe … but the psychological impact of what happened will take years to overcome.”

Amina has since been afraid to return to school. Her family tried taking her back once, but she left early, unable to bear the sound of the gunfire.

“She is now afraid of the school itself. She keeps dreaming about her classmate lying there with blood running from her,” Khader said.

He said the incident had also left him afraid for the rest of his children and his wife, with Israeli air raids, random gunfire and shelling continuing to affect streets near the school.

“We are confused about what to do. Do we keep our children away from school and deprive them of their education, or do we send them out, knowing that they could be targeted at any moment?” Khader said. “A student needs stability to be able to learn. But we have no stability, and there are no alternatives.”

articles.title: Bernie Sanders warns Oracle, Nvidia and other technology companies on expenditure that has wiped billions from their market value; says: Don’t come begging to taxpayers, you ...
articles.summary: Senator Bernie Sanders has a warning for technology companies on their ballooning AI expenditure.
articles.body: Senator Bernie Sanders has a warning for technology companies on their ballooning AI expenditure. In the last few quarters, Silicon Valley's biggest technology companies -- Microsoft, Meta, Google, Amazon, SpaceX, Oracle and Nvidia -- have increased their capital expenditure by billions. Wall Street has not taken this kindly, so much so that it has wiped out billions from their stock value. According to a report in Reuters, "More than $2 trillion in market value is set to be wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 this month, as Big Tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured ​into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough."Hitting at rising AI debt, Senator Bernie Sanders slammed technology companies for what he called their risky AI bets. In a post on X, formerly Twitter, he told these companies not to come to taxpayers if their bet fails to deliver. "Companies like Microsoft, Meta, Google, Amazon, SpaceX, Oracle & Nvidia have racked up $3 trillion in debt on a high-stakes gamble on AI. Big Tech Oligarchs: If your AI bet fails, don’t come begging to taxpayers. You won’t be bailed out — period. End of Discussion," wrote Sanders.More than $2 trillion in market value is on track to be erased from the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 this month as Big Tech earnings intensify investor questions over whether the enormous sums being poured into artificial intelligence will deliver returns quickly enough. The Nasdaq 100 has already fallen more than 5.8% so far in October as the AI trade has hit turbulence. Hyperscalers including Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon.com have raised their spending forecasts further while racing to expand AI infrastructure.$2 trillion-plus wiped out from Nasdaq 100Hyperscalers Meta, Google-parent Alphabet, and Amazon have all raised their forward-looking spending projections in recent months, committing hundreds of billions to compute clusters, custom chips, and data center infrastructure. However, with benchmark interest rates remaining elevated, Wall Street is growing increasingly uneasy about the rising cost of servicing capital investments that may take years to deliver meaningful profit margins.The reckoning was felt sharply on Thursday, when Alphabet suffered its largest single-day percentage decline on record. Investors reacted to slowing growth in the company's core search advertising unit alongside a steep rise in cash burn. Concurrently, Meta rattled markets with plans for a record $97.5 billion capital raise, sparking fears of equity dilution and raising concerns that tech giants may soon lean heavily on external financing to fund the AI arms race.AI companies’ growing reliance on debt funding is emerging as a fresh risk for investors, challenging the long-held view that the firms at the center of the boom are insulated from broader macroeconomic pressures. The concern is spreading beyond equities into credit markets, where investors are starting to price in the possibility that higher financing costs, combined with slower returns on AI spending, could squeeze companies previously regarded as relatively protected.Microsoft and SpaceX offered some relief from the gloom, delivering results that suggested AI spending is beginning to pay off. Microsoft posted quarterly results that suggested commercial AI applications are beginning to translate into revenue gains, offering a rare bright spot amid the tech sector selloff."It may be that we've overestimated how strong the growth might be, but they're not going negative in aggregate," John Bilton, global head of strategic research for multi-asset solutions at JPMorgan Asset Management, told Reuters. "We have an insatiable and growing demand for data," he added.Market focus now turns to next week, when Apple is scheduled to report its quarterly earnings, followed by Nvidia in mid-November. Nvidia's forward guidance, in particular, is viewed by analysts as the definitive litmus test for whether hardware demand can withstand cooling sentiment across the broader tech landscape.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Britain must acknowledge complicated history’: PM Burnham signals possible apology for UK’s role in slave trade
articles.summary: The UK could issue its first apology for its role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham stressing the need for Britain to
articles.body: The UK could issue its first apology for its role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham stressing the need for Britain to acknowledge its “complicated history” to safeguard the Commonwealth, a grouping of 56 independent nations that evolved from the British Empire.“For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery. By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," he wrote in The Guardian on Saturday.Burnham said his government would begin a “structured dialogue” with those affected by slavery and consider calls for a formal state apology, but would continue to resist demands for reparations.“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” he added.Instead, he pledged to address contemporary challenges facing Commonwealth nations, including mounting debt in developing countries. He also promised to work with wealthy nations and investors to help vulnerable countries repay their debts over longer periods and at lower interest rates.The remarks come as Britain seeks to strengthen ties with Commonwealth allies amid global economic, environmental and military challenges. Burnham is due to visit Antigua and Barbuda next week for a meeting of Commonwealth leaders.His position also comes amid growing calls, particularly from younger voters and activists, for Britain to "confront" its colonial past. In 2020, anti-racism protesters in Bristol pulled down a statue of Edward Colston, a merchant and former deputy governor of the Royal African Company, which transported enslaved people to English colonies in the Americas.While UK politicians have traditionally highlighted Britain's role in abolishing the slave trade in 1807 and slavery across the British Empire in 1833, Burnham stressed the need to acknowledge the country's role in the trade itself.“We are a country where brave people led the way in abolishing slavery, but we are also a country that participated in the trade in human lives," Burnham wrote.“The trans-Atlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. … I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognize the way it still shapes our world today.”(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Paycheck to paycheck’: Texas border voters shed parties amid economic woes
articles.summary: Voters reassess 2024 swing towards Trump as Republicans and Democrats grapple for Rio Grande Valley votes.
articles.body:
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Jesus Robles sells mechanical bulls.

Mainstays of bars and dance halls, once used to train rodeo riders, the bucking behemoths point to the Rio Grande Valley’s history, where Mexican and Texan Ranchero culture have long intertwined.

But the business has also been a nagging reminder of Robles’s 2024 vote, when he cast his ballot for US President Donald Trump, expecting an economic boost that would allow the company to flourish.

“I have lost tonnes of business due to our president right now,” he said, blaming Trump’s tariffs and rising fuel prices . “I ship a lot. The price of freight has doubled…. Some of my clients have been affected by immigration raids.”

Voters like Robles in 2024 helped reinforce the notion that the Rio Grande Valley, a Latino-dominated area long seen as reliably Democratic, was shifting Republican, bucking liberal hopes the ever-growing demographic would finally turn Texas blue.

His about-face in 2026, he said, underscored that no party should take voters in the region for granted.

“We focus on other countries. We focus on taxes,” said Robles, who cast his ballot on the final day of early voting in Alamo, Texas, about 50km (30 miles) from the US-Mexico border.

“But at the end of the day, I don’t feel none of these governments really help us, the people,” he added. “Because trust me, we work hard, the middle-class people work hard, and we’re the ones that get screwed the most.”

The Rio Grande Valley has become a battleground within a battleground this election season, with Republicans eyeing Trump’s 2024 gains – in which he won 14 of the 18 counties along the US-Mexico border – as evidence of a wider red shift.

They have set their sights on flipping at least two Democratic-controlled seats along the border, currently held by Representatives Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar, while holding onto a third, held by Republican Monica de la Cruz.

Democrats, riding on Trump’s high disapproval ratings among Latinos, who account for about 40 percent of the state’s population, are hoping to elect the first member of the party to statewide office in Texas since 1994. Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is running against Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, meanwhile, is seeking to unseat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.

While once considered a Democratic workhorse, the Rio Grande Valley has found itself increasingly out of step with both political parties, according to Alvaro Corral, an assistant professor of politics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.

Many have drifted away from a Democratic Party once embodied in figures like former President Bill Clinton, who captured “a mixture of traditional working-class economic platform that we associate with the Democratic Party, the New Deal Democrat sort of style, mixed with a little bit of, like, social conservatism, and being quite law-and-order focused”, Corral explained.

Some voters, in turn, found common ground in the religiously-dominated economic populism of Trump’s Republican Party, Corral said, only to find themselves alienated by his administration’s aggressive domestic immigration enforcement and a lack of pocketbook relief.

At the Alamo polling site, 40-year-old Natalie, an education worker who declined to give her last name out of professional concern, grimaced when she recounted her 2024 vote.

“I did vote for Trump,” she said. “It was immigration and the economy.”

But seeing her students grapple with family separation from Trump’s mass deportation drive , and watching the price of diesel to fuel her truck continue to tick up amid the US-Israel war on Iran, made her come to regret her vote.

“I just want people with empathy,” she said.

Voter Gabriel Ruiz pointed to the high cost of housing as a unifying issue, noting houses can cost between $400,000 and $500,000, a rate previously unheard of in the valley.

He said it has become common for voters to think beyond a party.

“It’s always going to be about the economy, job growth, being able to keep jobs here, and for the American people to flourish on their own and be able to afford housing, healthcare,” the 24-year-old said.

Michael Mireles, the director of civil engagement at La Union Del Pueblo Entero (LUPE), a local organisation that works to turn out Latino voters, said 2024 was, in part, a result of Democrats failing to conduct meaningful outreach in the Rio Grande Valley.

Only about 40 percent of registered voters cast ballots that year.

“Democrats in the last cycle, they were not trying to reach new voters. They were not trying to talk to people who are typically left out of Valley politics, which I think is a huge mistake,” he said.

“Because the work that needs to happen is with the people who have not been activated politically.”

Advocates believe the region is ripe for that kind of engagement.

The poverty level in the Rio Grande Valley hovers around 21 percent, the highest rate in the state and twice the national rate. It has remained nearly unchanged for a decade. As of 2023, about 37 percent of Rio Grande Valley residents did not have health insurance.

The Rio Grande Valley also has the highest concentration of so-called “colonias” of any part of the state. Colonias began as informal settlements in the 1950s, with the majority of modern residents US citizens.

About 1,200 colonias in the area are typically unincorporated neighbourhoods, meaning they do not fall under local jurisdictions and can lack basic infrastructure.

LUPE is among the groups that do voter outreach and education in those neighbourhoods.

Speaking to Al Jazeera from her home on the Erling colonia in Donna, Texas, 36-year-old Angeles Arguelles recounted not taking her sick children to the doctor recently because she could not afford the medication. Her husband works two jobs as a dishwasher, and the family has no insurance.

Despite being a US citizen, she said she has never voted.

“It just feels corrupt,” she said. “I just keep to myself and my family.”

At a nearby colonia in the city of Edinburg, 52-year-old Mario Hernandez, a restaurant worker, said his neighbourhood has become increasingly politically engaged.

“I’m not a Republican. I’m not Democrat. But it depends on who it is,” he said.

Hernandez said he had cast his ballot for all Democrats this year, motivated in part by concerns for his neighbours without health insurance.

“A lot of elderly can’t survive on their income,” he said. “Most of us live paycheck to paycheck here.”

articles.title: How TikTok and Halloween made Haworth an autumn destination
articles.summary: Queues outside shops are a regular sight in the village after influencers posted about its beauty.
articles.body:
With its dramatic landscapes and links to the Brontë sisters, Haworth has long been a popular destination for tourists.

But recently, the West Yorkshire village has been busier than ever, according to some residents and business owners, and is now attracting a new type of visitor - one brought in by how picturesque the place looks on social media, particularly during autumn.

A quick search on platforms like TikTok or Instagram shows a whole host of content promoting Haworth as a must-visit this October.

Posts also highlight the queues that can form outside shops, especially during the weekend.

The businesses lining the village's cobbled main street have embraced Halloween with colourful window displays, and none more so than The Cabinet of Curiosities.

The Victorian-style apothecary now sells a range of gifts, including soaps and candles, and its suitably spooky decor has made it something of a hit on social media, causing queues of people to line up, waiting to snap a picture or look inside.

Karen Roberts has worked at The Cabinet of Curiosities for nearly 20 years and says the shop has been especially busy this year.

"It suddenly started about six weeks ago to the point where we've had queues outside every weekend waiting to come in," she says.

"This week, with it being half-term, we've literally had people outside every day."

Although the business previously had a social media presence, she thinks the reason it "all blew up like this" is due to the sheer amount of people posting independently about the shop, and the village, on their own accounts.

"We've always let people film, we've never had a problem with that, but definitely people are asking me now, can they come in and film?," she explains.

"Then they share it, and every day you turn on Facebook and you go, 'oh my God, there is more'."

Many customers know about the connection to the Brontë family, and the parsonage where they lived is now a museum.

Emerald Fennell's 2026 adaption of Wuthering Heights, starring Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi, also sparked an interest in Brontë country.

And while increased footfall brings positives, there are downsides to social media stardom for the village, Roberts adds, highlighting a lack of parking as a main issue.

"There's certainly a downside. If you saw the bins at the end of the day, it is ridiculous."

By mid-morning a queue has formed outside The Cabinet of Curiosities, with the shop admitting small groups at a time.

Angela and Davinia Torres are bundled up against the elements. The pair are visiting the UK from Gran Canaria, and say the "beauty of the village" was the main draw.

"I always saw images and videos, TikToks and social media generally," Angela explains.

"We love to live the Halloween vibes, autumn. It's simply beautiful. The landscapes, everything, really."

Enjoying a day off work, Ella and Brian Thomas travelled from Greater Manchester to visit Haworth, inspired by a friend's Instagram post.

"With Wuthering Heights coming out, I think a lot of people have been seeing it on TikTok and making videos, so it was me who suggested to come here," Ella says.

The couple wanted to find somewhere "nice and autumnal" for a walk, and say they've previously visited York and Edinburgh for a "similar vibe".

"I knew it was the home of the Brontës, but I didn't know much more of the history than that," Brian explains.

Although they struggled to park at first, both agreed that "it was to be expected" that visiting during school half-term would be busier.

Standing below the steps to St Michael and All Angels Church, friends Hannah and Isa say the village is "busy today, but not as busy as we thought it would be".

They were planning on visiting earlier in the month, but decided against it when they saw long queues documented on social media.

"We have seen on TikTok people queuing up outside. Even tiny little shops, not necessarily restaurants," Hannah says.

According to Isa, the pair decided to visit on a weekday "because we've seen weekends are a bit crazy".

Further down Main Street, Claire Austin runs Silverland with Passion, her family jewellery business.

"We've had such a different influx of people," she says.

"We have people that come from far and wide. They've never seen a village that's on a big steep hill with so many businesses and residential properties."

It's common to see people live-streaming their walk along the street, or photographing the surrounding buildings, which she says "is so nice to see".

"Because there's been so many films here, people like to have pictures taken and, sort of re-enact things on the street, which is fantastic to see.

"It's a great little community, all the businesses work really hard together to make sure that every visitor has the best possible experience."

However, increased footfall often goes hand-in-hand with an increase of vehicles, she notes, with the village not necessarily "built for the amount of people" visiting.

Corine Farrell works at boutique gift shop Betty Moore, and is a Haworth resident.

A lack of visitor parking can cause problems for those who live in the village, she says, as they can end up dodging cars that "are parked not the way they should be".

"I struggle to get in and out of my street. The Airbnbs are full all the time.

"So those kind of things impact our daily life. Like everything, there's a positive and a negative.

"But it's nice that people come to the village and are respectful when they are here."

articles.title: A Georgia shopper won $975,000 over a fall at Walmart in 2020, but her lawyer compared pain damages with an expert's $8,000 daily fee; on October 29, an appeals court overturned the verdict and ordered a new trial
articles.summary: A Georgia woman who won $975,000 in compensation after a fall at a Walmart store in 2020 will have to go through another trial after a US appeals court
articles.body: A Georgia woman who won $975,000 in compensation after a fall at a Walmart store in 2020 will have to go through another trial after a US appeals court overturned the verdict on Thursday. The court found that her lawyer had used unrelated figures, including an expert witness's $8,000 daily fee, to suggest how much money the woman should receive for pain and suffering. The judges ruled that these comparisons were not permitted under Georgia's revised law and could have influenced the jury's decision.According to the judgment, the case involved Ruby Medders, who said she injured her knee and ankle after slipping and falling during a visit to a Walmart store in Valdosta, Georgia, in November 2020. She filed a lawsuit against the retailer in September 2022, seeking compensation for her injuries.Medders already had knee problems before the incident. However, she claimed that her pain became worse after the fall and eventually required surgery. Walmart disputed this, arguing that her knee condition existed before the accident and that the fall had not made the later operations necessary.Both sides presented medical experts when the case went to trial in January this year. During the lawyer's final arguments to the jury, a disagreement arose over how compensation for pain and suffering should be calculated. That disagreement eventually became the main reason the verdict was overturned.Expert's $8,000 daily fee During the trial, Medders' lawyer questioned a medical expert called by Walmart. The questioning included how much the doctor charged for providing expert testimony.The doctor charged $2,000 an hour for expert work and $8,000 for a full day at trial. These figures were presented to the jury as part of the evidence.Later, while asking the jury to consider compensation for Medders' pain and suffering, her lawyer referred to the doctor's earnings. He pointed out that the expert would have charged $8,000 a day for attending court.Walmart's lawyers immediately objected arguing that the doctor's professional fees had no meaningful connection to the pain Medders claimed to have experienced.The trial judge heard arguments from both sides but allowed Medders' lawyer to continue. The judge reasoned that the expert's fees had already been discussed during the trial and were therefore part of the evidence.The lawyer then suggested that the doctor's daily fee would amount to about $3 million a year. Walmart objected again, describing the figures as phantom numbers.It asked the judge either to declare a mistrial or to give the jury instructions correcting the impression created by the argument. Both requests were rejected.Medders' lawyer subsequently suggested another way of calculating compensation, using hourly figures between $7.25 and $12.15, closer to minimum-wage rates. Walmart also objected to this comparison. Despite the objections, the case went to the jury, which awarded Medders $975,000.Appeals court rejected lawyer's comparisonsWalmart challenged the verdict, arguing that the trial judge had failed to apply changes made to Georgia law in April 2025.The revised law deals with how lawyers can argue about compensation for losses that do not have a direct financial value, such as physical pain, emotional distress, and suffering. These are known as noneconomic damages.The law allows lawyers to suggest monetary amounts for such suffering, but their arguments must have a rational connection to the evidence about the injured person's condition.The appeals court found that comparing Medders' pain with an expert's professional earnings did not meet this requirement. It reached the same conclusion about the minimum-wage figures.The judges explained that the fact a figure had been mentioned during a trial did not automatically make it suitable for calculating compensation.However, the court clarified that lawyers were not completely prohibited from suggesting hourly or daily amounts for pain and suffering. Such calculations could still be used if they were properly connected to the evidence.Overturning of the $975,000 verdict The appeals court also examined whether the disputed arguments could have affected the amount awarded by the jury. According to the judgment, Medders had sought $186,000 for medical bills. Her lawyer also requested approximately $950,000 for non-economic damages and suggested that an appropriate total award could be $1,136,000. The jury ultimately awarded $975,000.The judges concluded that the improper comparisons could have influenced that decision, particularly because the trial court had not taken steps to correct them after Walmart objected. The Court of Appeals of Georgia therefore overturned the judgment and ordered a new trial. The case will now return to the lower court for another trial.You use AI every day. articles.title: From France to Portugal, Europe is protesting: How rising rents, living costs are fuelling anger
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: On Halloween, France is bracing for something far more unsettling than the usual festivities.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: On Halloween, France is bracing for something far more unsettling than the usual festivities. Thousands are expected to take to the streets on Saturday, as 70,000 police and gendarmes are mobilised across the country amid fears of fresh unrest. Shops have boarded up, security has been tightened and authorities are seeking to prevent a repeat of the violence that erupted earlier this month. Behind the protests lies a familiar frustration: rising living costs, strained public services and the growing difficulty of making ends meet.The anger is not confined to France. Europe has long been associated with high living standards, strong social security and the promise of a comfortable life. But for a growing number of its residents, that promise is being tested by the monthly arithmetic of survival. In Lisbon, two people earning local salaries and sharing a three-bedroom city-centre apartment are left with just €253 after paying rent. In Milan, the amount is €697. Across the continent, rising housing costs, expensive essentials, stagnant wages and mounting pressure on public services are turning household budgets into a source of public discontent.From housing demonstrations in Spain and Portugal to protests over wages, education and government policies in France, Italy, Belgium and Germany, the grievances differ but point to a broader unease. The question confronting Europe is no longer simply whether people have jobs or earn a salary, but whether their earnings are enough to afford the life they were promised.The contrast with northern Europe is stark. The same calculation leaves a working couple in Zurich with €9,140 after rent, while €8,783 remains in Geneva.These figures, drawn from Deutsche Bank Research Institute's Mapping the World's Prices 2026 report, compare the combined net salaries of two local earners with the monthly rent of a three-bedroom city-centre apartment. They do not account for groceries, electricity, transport, healthcare or other household expenses. The calculation illustrates the gap between local earnings and city-centre rents rather than the actual spending patterns of every household.The difference is not simply about how much people earn. Zurich has Europe's highest rent in the comparison, at €5,502, but also the highest average net salary, at €7,321 per person. Lisbon, by contrast, has an average net salary of €1,408 against a city-centre rent of €2,561. In 11 of the 28 European cities examined, rent exceeds one local net salary.The difference is not simply about how much people earn. Zurich has Europe's highest rent in the comparison, at €5,502, but also the highest average net salary, at €7,321 per person. Lisbon, by contrast, has an average net salary of €1,408 against a city-centre rent of €2,561. In 11 of the 28 European cities examined, rent exceeds one local net salary.The rent-to-income gap is only the beginningThe housing burden becomes clearer when measured against household income rather than nominal rent. Eurostat's Housing in Europe 2025 report found that EU households spent an average of 19% of their disposable income on housing in 2024. The share was 36% in Greece, 26% in Denmark and 25% in both Germany and Sweden. For households at risk of poverty, housing consumed 37% of disposable income across the EU.The longer-term trend is equally revealing. Between 2010 and 2024, house prices across the EU increased by 53%, while rents rose 25%. General consumer prices increased by 39% during the same period. In other words, housing prices outpaced overall inflation, adding to the pressure on tenants and prospective homeowners.Greece presents one of the clearest examples of the squeeze. Apart from having the highest housing expenditure relative to disposable income among the countries listed, it also recorded a 43% share of people living in households with arrears on mortgage, rent or utility bills in 2024, the highest in the EU.For younger Europeans, the challenge extends beyond finding a job. Eurostat's 2025 data show that 9.1% of people aged 15-29 lived in households spending at least 40% of disposable income on housing. The figure was 25.6% in Greece and 26.9% in Denmark. Across the EU, 26.9% of young people aged 15-29 lived in overcrowded households.The problem is not confined to rent. Food, another unavoidable household expense, accounts for a substantial share of monthly expenditure. Eurostat estimates that food and non-alcoholic beverages accounted for 13.1% of total household expenditure in the EU in 2024. The share was 18.1% in Portugal, 15.7% in Greece and 14.7% in Italy. In Germany, it was 11.1%, while France recorded 12%.Food may be cheaper, but is it affordable?A comparison of food prices across Europe also reveals a gap between the cost of a grocery basket and the ability to pay for it.Eurostat's 2025 comparative price-level index, which sets the EU average at 100, puts food and non-alcoholic beverage prices at 106.8 in France, 105.3 in Greece, 104.5 in Belgium, 102.4 in Germany, 102 in Portugal and 101.1 in Italy. Spain, at 95.3, is below the EU average. Romania recorded one of the lowest levels, at 79.8.The comparison also exposes why cheaper groceries do not automatically translate into greater affordability. Romanian households, for example, spent 23% of their total expenditure on food and non-alcoholic beverages in 2024, compared with the EU average of 13.1%. Portugal's share was 18.1%. Lower prices can still absorb a larger portion of household budgets when incomes are lower.The latest inflation figures add another layer. Eurostat reported that eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September 2026, up from 3.2% in August. Energy prices rose 18.9% year-on-year, while food, alcohol and tobacco prices increased 1.3%. Within the food category, unprocessed food inflation was 4%.The distinction between inflation and price levels is important. Slower inflation does not mean groceries have become cheaper. It means prices are increasing at a slower pace. The accumulated increases of previous years remain part of household bills.Why are Europeans taking to the streets?The data help explain the economic pressure, but the protests have several immediate triggers. They are not one coordinated European movement, nor are they driven by a single political ideology.In France, demonstrations that began with complaints about school infrastructure, overcrowding and teacher shortages expanded into wider protests over living costs, wages and public services. The country has also witnessed clashes during demonstrations, prompting large-scale security deployments.In Spain and Portugal, housing affordability has become a central grievance. Protesters have opposed rising rents and the pressure of tourism on local housing markets. In Portugal, demonstrations have also demanded higher wages and pensions. In Italy, protests have brought together demands relating to employment, healthcare, education, housing and opposition to rearmament.Belgium has witnessed demonstrations over living costs and education expenses, while Albania's protests have focused on corruption and government accountability. In Germany, youth-led demonstrations have raised demands concerning schools, housing and climate spending, alongside opposition to restoring compulsory military service."Every protest has its own dynamics. One needs to examine the specific reasons behind demonstrations in Spain, France, Belgium or any other country because each has its own history, economic difficulties and political context," Gulshan Sachdeva, Professor of European Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), told TOI.However, he believes there is a common economic thread connecting several of these demonstrations."What we are witnessing is a combination of several crises: economic stagnation, rising living costs, housing shortages, demographic pressures, immigration-related anxieties and changing political dynamics. It is a broad cocktail of problems rather than a single cause of public unrest," Prof. Sachdeva said.The pressure on housing is particularly visible in southern Europe, where the growth of tourism has added to competition for residential properties. Sachdeva said local residents in cities such as Barcelona and Madrid increasingly feel priced out of their neighbourhoods as properties are used for tourism and short-term rentals."The cost of living has risen, housing has become increasingly unaffordable, and younger people feel that the welfare state they inherited is no longer providing the same level of support," he said.A crisis of growth, public spending and political trustEconomists and political analysts say the problem extends beyond household expenditure. Years of weak economic growth, demographic changes, pressure on government finances and growing competition from emerging economies have reduced the room available to European governments to respond to public demands.Rajan Kumar, Professor at JNU, said the economic difficulties have been compounded by the Ukraine conflict and Europe's move away from Russian energy supplies. Higher energy costs have affected production, transportation and other commodities, adding to the cost pressures faced by households and businesses.The pressure on government finances is another part of the problem. Under the EU's fiscal framework, the reference values for government deficits and public debt are 3% and 60% of GDP, respectively. These are not absolute spending ceilings, but countries exceeding them can face corrective procedures. France's public debt, for instance, stood at 119.1% of GDP at the end of the second quarter of 2026. Greece, Italy and Belgium were also above the 100% mark.Kumar argued that governments are finding it difficult to maintain welfare expenditure while responding to demands for higher defence spending. More money allocated to defence could put additional pressure on other spending priorities, including education and healthcare.He also pointed to Europe's ageing population, declining working-age population and loss of some of its traditional industrial and technological advantages to countries such as China and India."The real issue is that the centre of gravity of global economic development has shifted towards countries such as India and China. Europe's technological and industrial dominance is no longer what it used to be."The growing political focus on immigration is another dimension. Both experts cautioned against treating migration as the primary cause of economic distress. Sachdeva said younger Europeans are more concerned about affordable accommodation, educational infrastructure and employment opportunities than about migrants taking their jobs."The younger generation is not necessarily worried about outsiders taking their jobs. Its immediate concerns are better university infrastructure, improved educational facilities, better employment prospects and affordable housing."He also rejected the argument that generous welfare systems have made young Europeans unwilling to work. Rather, he said, the problem is that employment opportunities and public services are not expanding at the pace people expect.Meanwhile, right-wing political parties have increasingly used immigration and national identity as political issues, sometimes directing public anger towards migrants instead of the underlying economic problems.France's warning and the road aheadThe economic pressure is particularly visible in France, where finance minister Roland Lescure warned on October 30 that the country needed a budgetary turnaround to avoid a deeper crisis.France's GDP contracted by 0.1% in the third quarter of 2026, following stagnation in the second quarter and a 0.2% contraction in the first. Lescure warned that without the proposed budgetary correction, the country was "headed straight for a wall"."For three quarters now, there has been no growth. If we fail to achieve the turnaround outlined in the budget, we are headed straight for a wall. The conclusion to be drawn from all this is that, as of 2026, the French economy is at a standstill. "But an economic turnaround alone may not guarantee social stability. Sachdeva pointed out that protests are also being shaped by domestic electoral calculations, with political parties using public discontent to advance their interests.With elections approaching, Spain is set to vote on November 29, 2026, followed by France’s presidential election on April 18, 2027, with a possible May 2 runoff. Greece is expected to hold parliamentary elections in spring 2027, while Italy’s election is due by December 22, 2027, though a snap poll in April 2027 is possible.There is no clear timeline for when Europe will return to relative social and political calm. While protests may subside in individual countries, the pressures driving them are unlikely to disappear through a change of government or a temporary slowdown in inflation. articles.title: UK PM rejects slavery reparations despite Caribbean demands, open to formal apology
articles.summary: British prime minister Andy Burnham has indicated that he is willing to consider calls for a formal apology for Britain's involvement in the transatlantic
articles.body: British prime minister Andy Burnham has indicated that he is willing to consider calls for a formal apology for Britain's involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out paying financial reparations for historical injustices.In an article published in The Guardian, Burnham said his government was prepared to engage with countries and communities affected by slavery through a "structured dialogue". He made the remarks ahead of next week's Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda, where Caribbean leaders are expected to push for reparations."Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them," Burnham wrote.However, he rejected the argument that people living in Britain today should be financially responsible for crimes committed centuries ago."I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," he said.The transatlantic slave trade lasted from the 15th to the 19th century, during which millions of Africans were captured, transported and sold into slavery by European traders. According to the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database, Britain transported an estimated 3.2 million Africans across the Atlantic. At least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and forced into the trade.The issue is expected to feature prominently at the Commonwealth summit, with Caribbean nations seeking reparations for the lasting impact of slavery and colonial exploitation. Their demands have included debt relief, development funding, better access to education and healthcare, and financial support to deal with climate change.King Charles, who is currently touring the Caribbean, has also acknowledged the suffering caused by slavery. Ahead of the summit, he said it was "only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past".Alongside the proposal for dialogue, Burnham said he wanted Britain to take practical steps to help vulnerable countries manage their financial difficulties.He said he hoped to "launch a new drive on debt", including measures that would allow more vulnerable nations to "repay over a longer time period and with better rates".Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne welcomed Burnham's comments and proposals for practical assistance. However, he made clear that the Caribbean's demand for reparatory justice had not changed."The Caribbean's longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged," Browne said in a Facebook post.You use AI every day. articles.title: Evacuated Ukrainians from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Belarus
articles.summary: Residents left the devastated city on Friday following a ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
articles.body:
People evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have arrived in Belarus and are expected back in Ukraine later on Saturday, authorities have said.

Residents of the frontline city had been trapped without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.

The evacuees were taken out of Oleshky on Friday during a local ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.

Planes carrying the residents landed in the city of Gomel on Saturday morning, according to Belarusian state media and a senior Ukrainian official.

"The last, fourth plane landed in Gomel (Belarus). In a few hours, all Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky, together with the Ukrainian delegation, will be on Ukrainian territory," said David Arakhamia, a key Ukrainian official.

The state-owned Belarusian news agency Belta reported a bus convoy of Oleshky residents had left Gomel airport and was heading towards the Ukrainian border.

A humanitarian ceasefire took effect across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday, providing the first few days of peace in the area in four years, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Conditions had become so desperate in Oleshky that not only was getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escape was highly dangerous because the routes out had been mined and subject to drone attack.

One resident who fled the city three weeks earlier told the BBC he had walked through 24km (15 miles) of minefields to get to safety.

The ceasefire allowed the road out of the city to be cleared of mines and will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.

Residents had a four-hour window to leave before a convoy of 25 buses, with space for 750 people, left the town on Friday afternoon - along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay in the war-torn city, despite widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

Before the war, Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning that those who decided to stay "will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance".

Ukrainian military positions lie just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky but evacuees first had to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa, where they flew to Gomel.

Bridges across the nearby River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank has been mined and is dangerous.

Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.

Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.

The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.

But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.

Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.

articles.title: UN closes Somalia mission, ending three decades of political engagement
articles.summary: Somalia hails the UN mission’s closure as a milestone amid political tensions and cuts to international support.
articles.body:
The United Nations has closed its political mission in Somalia , ending more than three decades of efforts to help the country rebuild after civil war.

The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) ceased operations on Saturday after completing a two-year transition requested by the Somali government, the mission said in a statement on X.

Its responsibilities have been gradually transferred to Somali institutions, UN agencies and the UN office supporting African Union (AU) troops under a roadmap agreed between Somalia and the UN.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Somalia’s progress but called for continued international backing amid political, security and humanitarian challenges.

The closure follows years of sometimes strained relations between Somali governments and the UN mission, whose involvement in domestic politics has repeatedly prompted accusations of interference.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s government formally requested its withdrawal in 2024.

At a farewell ceremony in Mogadishu on Monday, Deputy Prime Minister Saleh Ahmed Jama hailed the closure as a “day of victory”, saying Somalia was now leaving behind the “era of transition”.

The departure comes as international support for Somalia is shrinking, even as the country faces deep political divisions and continuing violence.

Opposition leaders reject the government’s position that constitutional changes allow President Mohamud and parliament to remain in office until 2027.

Relations with some regional leaders are also strained, while al-Shabab , an armed group linked to al-Qaeda, continues to fight government forces.

The UN mission previously helped rival leaders reach election agreements, but no replacement for its mediation role has been agreed.

Mohamud has invited political opponents to talks, although major opposition groups have yet to confirm their attendance.

UN humanitarian and development agencies remain in Somalia, but their funding has been hard-hit by cuts to international aid.

In August, the UN children’s agency said 205 health and nutrition facilities had closed because of aid cuts.

AU troops also remain to support Somali forces against al-Shabab, but their operations depend heavily on a separate UN office, UNSOS, providing food, fuel, medical care and transport.

However, that vital support could end by December 2027 under a US-backed plan to close the UN office providing it, the Reuters news agency reported in September.

articles.title: US midterms 2026: Judge blocks Trump admin from threatening election workers over voter data demands
articles.summary: A federal judge has prohibited the US Justice Department from intimidating election officials to remove non-citizen voters ahead of the midterm elections, citing public interest and election integrity.
articles.body: A US federal judge has barred the Justice Department from threatening state and local election officials with prosecution for refusing to follow the Trump administration's demands over voters suspected of being non-citizens.US District Judge Trina Thompson issued the temporary restraining order on Friday, ruling that the administration could not use its list of alleged non-citizen voters to direct local officials to change how they administer elections.The order prevents the federal government from demanding that election officials remove voters from state registration lists, reject ballots from specific voters or separate ballots cast in the midterm elections on the basis of the administration's list.Thompson said the Justice Department had overstepped by threatening prosecution against officials who did not cooperate with its election-related initiatives. The ruling followed a lawsuit filed by election workers' unions and other groups."The balance of the equities and public interest weigh in Plaintiffs' favor," Thompson wrote, citing the need for election officials and workers to perform their duties under federal law and established election procedures.The decision comes days before the November 3 midterm elections. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers, while Democrats are seeking to gain control of the House and potentially the Senate.The Trump administration has sought voter-registration data from states, arguing that stricter oversight is necessary to protect election security and public confidence in the voting process. However, its efforts have drawn criticism from election officials and political experts, who have raised concerns about federal interference in state and local election administration.Some election officials told Reuters they were preparing for possible federal intervention during the midterms.Trump has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections and continued to make false claims about the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden.You use AI every day. articles.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
articles.summary: The American-made interceptors are the only effective weapon for downing Russia's ballistic missiles.
articles.body:
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.

However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.

The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.

On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots – the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.

In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night.

He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day".

The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.

The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.

Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".

It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".

The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".

Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.

The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies that the country was running critically low on.

In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".

He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.

Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.

It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.

Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.

In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles - three weeks after offering the country such a right.
